source: Wang et al. (2025) Explore the Reasoning Capability of LLMs in the Chess Testbed (MATE)
finding: Frontier chat models were near chance at choosing between two expert-annotated candidate moves. A fine-tuned 8B model was far better.
numbers: Two-candidate choice, 1,000 test items per subset, zero-shot. MATE-ST: o1-preview 76.6%, gpt-4 60.0, claude-3.5-sonnet 54.9, gemini-1.5-pro 52.6; fine-tuned Llama-3-8B 95.2%. MATE-N (no explanation): o1-preview 56.4%, gpt-4o 46.4%.
limits: Puzzle-style choice between two plausible moves, not full games. Only one model fine-tuned. Chance is 50%.
agent_relevance: A general model comparing candidates without help is weak at chess. Do not trust the model to rank candidates; use a checker.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Explore the Reasoning Capability of LLMs in the Chess Testbed (MATE)
finding: Giving the model written strategy or tactic explanations raised accuracy a lot. Few-shot prompting changed little overall.
numbers: o1-mini zero-shot rises from the MATE-N baseline by 14 points (strategy), 24 (tactic), 34 (both). Few-shot: gpt-4 MATE-ST 60.0 to 68.1, claude-3.5-sonnet MATE-S 54.9 to 63.7; gemini-1.5-pro flat (52.6 to 50.4). With three candidates the fine-tuned model drops to 40.0 (N) and 56.1 (S).
limits: Gains vary by cell; the authors say few-shot does not substantially change results. Accuracy falls as candidates increase.
agent_relevance: Writing a short note per candidate helps comparison; more candidates hurt, which supports narrow candidate sets.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess (Grandmaster-Level Chess Without Search)
finding: A 270M transformer trained to predict Stockfish action values plays at grandmaster level with no explicit search. Strength needed scale.
numbers: 270M model: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans, 2299 tournament Elo, 93.5% puzzle accuracy, 69.4% action accuracy. 99M: 2007 Elo, 85.5% puzzles. GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct 1755 Elo, 66.5% puzzles. AlphaZero policy only 1620 Elo; AlphaZero with 400 MCTS sims 2502 Elo, 95.8% puzzles. Stockfish 16 2706.
limits: Trained on 10M games with 15.3B Stockfish labels (about 8,680 Stockfish-days). Elo vs bots only 2299. The value-based policy does one-step lookahead. No game history.
agent_relevance: Deep search can be amortized into a model, but only with engine-labelled data. A prompt-only agent cannot copy this; it needs a real search loop.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering Board Games by External and Internal Planning with Language Models
finding: A language model used inside external MCTS, or trained to write its own search tree in text, gained strength over the same model with no search.
numbers: 2.7B model, chess Elo (internal/external): searchless MAV 1367/2923; MCTS 100 sims 1435/2988; 250 sims 1542/3088; 500 sims 1592/3131; 1000 sims 1633/3157; 2000 sims 1707/3209. About 300 Elo from search overall. Internal search tree well-formed in 99.6% of 5,980 positions; strength rose with budget (breadth up to 4, depth up to 2). 100 to 1k simulations per move called comparable to human budgets.
limits: Model trained on game data, no natural language. External Elo not accurate for blitz. The 'human budget' claim is loose; no exact human node count given.
agent_relevance: Closest published case of a text-written search loop: shallow breadth and depth, strength grows with budget. Supports letting code run bounded search and record results.

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: Better Planning with Transformers via Search Dynamics Bootstrapping (Searchformer)
finding: Training a transformer on the full trace of A* search, then bootstrapping it to use fewer steps, beat training on the answer alone.
numbers: Sokoban, 200 unseen tasks, 45M params: solution-only 86.8% optimal; search-augmented 90.8%; Searchformer step 3 93.7% optimal. Uses on average 26.8% fewer search steps than A*. 5 to 10x smaller models and 10x less data than solution-only baselines. 3 bootstrap rounds, 32 samples per puzzle, keep shortest optimal; errors fall 40% (wrong) and 30% (non-optimal).
limits: Synthetic puzzles with a symbolic solver as teacher. Not chess. Needs a solver to make traces.
agent_relevance: Showing the search trace helps, and trimming to shorter traces that still work is possible. Supports logging and compressing our own search traces.

source: Gandhi et al. (2024) Stream of Search (SoS): Learning to Search in Language
finding: A small model trained on messy search streams (with dead ends and backtracking) solved Countdown better than one trained only on optimal paths.
numbers: Countdown, GPT-Neo 250M, held-out inputs: SoS 51.27% vs optimal-path 25.73%. STaR about +5%, APA about +6% (0.5127 to 0.5652 seen; 0.4900 to 0.5423 unseen). About 4% of problems no symbolic strategy solves were solved. 2.2 arithmetic errors per trajectory (0.7 after APA).
limits: One toy task. Needs a symbolic search algorithm to generate data. SoS slightly below the average of its training strategies.
agent_relevance: Training on traces that include mistakes and returns beats clean answers, but this is training, not prompting. For us: keep failed branches in the record.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Letting GPT-4 explore several partial thoughts, evaluate them and backtrack beat chain of thought on tasks that need lookahead.
numbers: Game of 24: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. Mini crosswords game success: IO 0%, CoT 1%, ToT 20%; ToT with no backtracking 5%, no pruning 5%. Creative writing coherence (1-10): IO 6.19, CoT 6.93, ToT 7.56. Cost per case, Game of 24: ToT $0.74 vs CoT best-of-100 $0.47. GPT-3.5 ToT only 19%.
limits: Three small tasks. 5 to 100x more tokens than CoT. Authors say search may not be needed where GPT-4 already does well.
agent_relevance: Removing backtracking cut crossword game success from 20% to 5%. Returning to earlier nodes matters, and so does pruning. Cost is the price.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Asking a model to review and revise its own answer without outside feedback did not help and often hurt. With an oracle label it looked good, because the label leaked.
numbers: No oracle, standard to round 2: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0, HotpotQA 49 to 43; Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 36.5. With oracle: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7. Debate at 6 responses 83.2 vs self-consistency 85.3 (GSM8K, GPT-3.5).
limits: Samples of 200 questions (100 for HotpotQA) for non-GPT-3.5 models; mixed temperatures. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K rose 88.0 to 90.0 in round 2. Self-correction may help in style or safety.
agent_relevance: Main warning for returning to a candidate: revisiting with no new real information does not deepen. Matches G2 and G3: revise only from checked output.

source: Wen, Tang, Anderson (2025) ChessQA: Evaluating Large Language Models for Chess Understanding
finding: Turning thinking on raised chess accuracy a lot, but short tactics stayed weak and board-state misreads were a main failure.
numbers: 50 tasks, 3,500 items; 15 LLMs, 23 configurations. GPT-5 thinking 79.3% (44.0% without); DeepSeek V3.1 39.6 to 56.4; Claude Sonnet 4 41.7 to 51.8. Average thinking gain +14.7 points. Short Tactics averaged 17.4%; Position Judgment best 40%. GPT-5 thinking used 9,142 tokens per task vs 1,236 without. Piece arrangement given: Claude 3.5 Haiku 14.5% to 23.5%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 24.1% to 31.0%.
limits: First-move scoring only, puzzles under 6 ply. Black-box, no tools. Cost estimates may be off.
agent_relevance: Thinking helps but costs about 7x the tokens. Errors begin in reading the board: restate the state exactly from code before any search.

source: Liu et al. (2025) ChessArena: A Chess Testbed for Evaluating Strategic Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs
finding: Thinking models rank higher, but none beat a weak human-level engine. Play gets worse over long games.
numbers: 13 LLMs, over 800 games, Glicko: Maia-1100 2220; o3 1948 (no legal moves given); Gemini-2.5-Pro 1819; random player 1524. Puzzles (1,008): Stockfish 98.4%, Maia-1100 74.6%, o3 55.6%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 14.0%, random 0.7%. o3 top-move rate 43.5% blindfold vs 62.0% standard. R1 and Doubao-Thinking declined beyond 90 turns. Qwen3-8B SFT+RL: 1335 to 1776 with legal moves given; legal rate 92.9%.
limits: Fine-tuned model weak without legal moves. Outcome filtering may keep flawed reasoning.
agent_relevance: Providing the legal-move list from code is worth a lot. Long contexts decay; keep state in code, not in the transcript.

source: Hwang et al. (2025) Can Large Language Models Develop Strategic Reasoning? Post-training Insights from Learning Chess
finding: RL with a dense chess-engine reward on small open models plateaued at 25 to 30% puzzle accuracy. The authors blame missing chess knowledge from pretraining.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Llama3.1-8B, GRPO 150 steps, 19.2k Lichess puzzle positions, reward from a 270M action-value net. Plateau about 25-30% vs 60-80% for human experts. Sparse rewards failed for 3B and Llama. Board-state accuracy 0.0% for all. About 979 o3 traces for SFT then RL: same plateau; Llama dropped.
limits: Authors call conclusions speculative; base models, not Instruct.
agent_relevance: Training to reason longer does not add knowledge the base lacks. A scaffold cannot either; it can only organize what is there.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) SPIN-Bench: How Well Do LLMs Plan Strategically and Reason Socially?
finding: Every LLM lost every chess game against even the weakest engine level. Reasoning models did best; tactical depth was the limit.
numbers: Chess top-3 move match: o3-mini 52.8%, Llama4 Maverick 51.3, o4-mini 50.5, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 49.5, DeepSeek R1 47.8, o1 45.9, GPT-4-turbo 38.7, GPT-4o 32.2, Llama-3.3-70b 25.4. Draw rate vs solver 0% for all. Internal Elo: o1-preview 1395, GPT-4-turbo 1265, GPT-4o 1255, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 1196. PDDL plan accuracy: o1 58.59%, GPT-4o 8.75%.
limits: Fixed prompt templates; internal Elo not comparable to human ratings; top-1 and top-5 not in the text read.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models help most where lookahead is needed, but are far from a depth-aware searcher. An external engine or checker is needed.

source: Extracting Search Trees from LLM Reasoning Traces Reveals Myopic Planning (2026)
finding: Reasoning models write out branches but act almost only on the first ply. Humans use deeper lookahead; these models do not.
numbers: 4x9 four-in-a-row, 27 models, 1,404 games; 14 models with open traces, 9,696 traces. Mean max depth 1.78 plies (range 1.00 to 3.48) vs 4 to 6 inferred for humans. Win rate on breadth beta 0.075 (p=0.0025); on depth beta -0.015 (p=0.82). Discount factor near zero for every model. Removing the chosen move's branch changed the move in 32.0% of cases; the largest unchosen branch 1.2%; final-decision paragraphs 2.1%. GPT-OSS-120B at high effort: bigger trees, more wins than at medium.
limits: One game; trees extracted by a GPT-5 judge; one fixed heuristic family.
agent_relevance: A direct test of progressive deepening in a model: deeper lines are written but not used. Our scaffold should make deep lines count through code, for example by scoring leaves.

source: Do Chess Explanations Reflect Model Decisions? Behavioral and Token-Level Tests of LLM Reasoning Faithfulness (2026)
finding: Chess explanations from LLMs mostly mirror the move already chosen. Human think-aloud shows abandoned candidates; LLM text compresses to one confident plan.
numbers: 200 Lichess endgame puzzles rated 500-2000. GPT-4.1-mini legal 0.512, exact match 0.082; Kimi-K2 legal 0.487; Llama-3.3-70B legal 0.068. Recovering the generated move from the masked explanation: top-1 0.379 to 0.398; the reference move only 0.056 to 0.091. On 25 perturbed puzzles the generated move changed 0.959. Human pilot transcripts averaged 560 words (n=3) vs 47.5 to 128.3 words for LLM conditions.
limits: Human pilot is tiny and unmatched. Associations, not causes. Hosted models are small ones.
agent_relevance: Written reasoning is not a record of how the move was chosen. Do not treat the explanation as proof of search.

source: Ciancarini and Pareschi (2026) What Counts as Strategic Reasoning? A Systematic Mapping of Chess Research on Humans, Engines, and Language Models
finding: Across 84 chess study families, planning, explanation and metacognition are under-studied; LLM work centers on state representation.
numbers: 84 core study families classified by agent type, reasoning stage and evaluation. The abstract page does not mention de Groot or progressive deepening.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; the PDF text could not be extracted.
agent_relevance: Suggests a gap: no study found that measures progressive deepening as such in LLM chess play.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) Can Large Language Models Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?
finding: Self-critique of plans lowered plan quality, and LLM verifiers gave many false positives (search summary only).
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Seen only in a search result summary; do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Same warning as Huang et al.: revisiting needs an outside verifier.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Forcing the model to continue with the word Wait when it tries to stop made it re-check and sometimes fix steps (abstract-level summary only).
numbers: Reported in the abstract: AIME24 from 50% to 57% with budget forcing; Qwen2.5-32B tuned on 1,000 examples. Not verified from the full text.
limits: Search snippet only.
agent_relevance: A cheap analog of returning to the same problem for more depth. Compare with our rule to doubt only on a signal (G1).

source: Deep Self-Evolving Reasoning (arXiv 2510.17498)
finding: Repeated solve, verify, refine cycles are framed as a Markov chain; surviving consecutive verification rejections signals correctness (search summary only).
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Search snippet only; authors not checked.
agent_relevance: A loop shape to test as a revisit operator; reliability depends on the verifier being independent.

source: TsuGO: Probing Search Efficiency in LLM Reasoning via Go Life-and-Death Problems (2026)
finding: Longer chains of thought do not mean better search. Strong models give the right candidate early attention and keep it; weak ones spread effort over shallow wrong branches.
numbers: 600 problems (200 per tier). A jump back to an earlier candidate counts as backtracking. Easy tier, accuracy / search efficiency, K=4 vs K=None: Gemini-3.1-Pro 80.0/47.3 vs 65.0/46.6; Kimi-K2.5 52.0/39.9 vs 27.8/26.4; MCTS/UCT 33.0/35.8 vs 5.0/13.1; KataGo 97.0/96.9 vs 49.0/53.3. Trace extraction by Gemini-2.5-Pro agreed 93 to 98% with experts.
limits: No correlation coefficients in the part read. First-move scoring only. Closed models expose summaries only. Robustness probe used 10 problems per model.
agent_relevance: Gives a metric for revisits and a goal: fund the right candidate early. Could audit our scaffold traces.

source: Reasoning is not search: a chess example (LessWrong essay)
finding: A first-person essay argues players find constraints, then moves that meet them, rather than brute-force search (search summary only).
numbers: None.
limits: Informal essay, not an empirical study; not opened.
agent_relevance: A competing view to progressive deepening; treat as a hypothesis only.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Explore the Reasoning Capability of LLMs in the Chess Testbed (MATE)
finding: The paper's headline 24.2% gain is relative, not absolute.
numbers: 95.2% vs 76.6% on MATE-ST zero-shot is 18.6 points absolute.
limits: Check the unit before comparing across papers.
agent_relevance: Store absolute gaps in our claims file.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess (Grandmaster-Level Chess Without Search)
finding: The searchless model still needs code-side rules at its edges.
numbers: Repeating move set to 50% win chance; Stockfish checks the top five moves when all exceed 99%. Elo vs bots (2299) is below vs humans (2895).
limits: Authors suggest humans resign or pools are miscalibrated.
agent_relevance: Even strong searchless policies need rule-based patches; a thinking scaffold should expect the same.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering Board Games by External and Internal Planning with Language Models
finding: Search stays reliable because malformed outputs get a value of minus infinity and are dropped.
numbers: Legal best action 0.999 on Lichess puzzles and 0.996 on out-of-distribution positions; correct updated board 1.000 / 0.996; about 10% of evaluated positions appeared in training.
limits: Training overlap not removed.
agent_relevance: Reject malformed branches by code instead of trusting the model's state tracking.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Part of earlier self-correction gains came from a weak first prompt, not from the correction step.
numbers: Oracle gains vanish without labels; GPT-4 HotpotQA 49 to 59 with oracle, 43 after two rounds without.
limits: Small samples.
agent_relevance: Compare any revisit operator against a strong one-shot prompt, not a weak one.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Ablations show both pruning and backtracking are needed on crosswords.
numbers: Word-level: ToT 60%; no pruning 41.5%; no backtracking 20%. Letter-level 78 / 65.4 / 54.6.
limits: Mini crosswords, 20 games.
agent_relevance: Revisit and prune should both be operators.

source: Liu et al. (2025) ChessArena: A Chess Testbed for Evaluating Strategic Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs
finding: Non-thinking models often guess from the last move when state is given only as a move list.
numbers: GPT-4.1 legal rate 97.5% with legal moves given vs 71.6% without (Blitz).
limits: Single prompt format.
agent_relevance: Give the board, not a move history.

source: Wen, Tang, Anderson (2025) ChessQA: Evaluating Large Language Models for Chess Understanding
finding: Error analysis of the best model found sound intermediate analysis ending in a wrong final move, and false claims that no answer exists.
numbers: Four failure modes: board hallucination; legality errors in short tactics; good analysis but wrong final move; claiming no answer.
limits: Analysis of GPT-5 thinking only.
agent_relevance: A final selection step done by code over analysed candidates would avoid the third failure.
